prompt: If the peer assessment marks seem incorrect,

options.text: students should mark the assignments again.
the tutor should check those assignments.
the marking criteria should be rewritten.

evidence: Sally says asking the students to repeat the marking may not change anything, so in that case the tutor would have to remark the assignments.
why: If the marks look wrong, the tutor must check and remark the affected assignments, which matches option B.
trap: A: Sally says repeating the student marking may not make any difference. C: The marking criteria should be reviewed carefully with students for the next assignment, not simply rewritten as the immediate solution.
explanation: The tutor, not the students, should recheck the questionable marking.

prompt: How were the presentations in the research project marked?

options.text: Students and lecturers marked all the presentations.
Students chose which presentations they wanted to mark.
Lecturers marked a selection of presentations.

evidence: Each student gave a short presentation, and every presentation was assessed individually by all participants, both students and lecturers.
why: All participants marked every presentation, so option A is the direct match.
trap: B: Students did not choose only selected presentations to assess. C: Lecturers did not mark only a subset; they assessed all the presentations along with the students.
explanation: Every presentation was marked by both groups: students and lecturers.

prompt: John and Cath's presentation plans are different in
evidence: They agree that their plans have the same three main sections and the same overall organisation, but they have chosen different sports examples to illustrate the injuries.
why: The structure and main points are the same; the examples are what differ, so option A is correct.
trap: B: They say their presentations are organised in the same way. C: They have included the same three main sections, so the main points are not the difference.
explanation: Their plans differ only in the sports examples used to illustrate possible injuries.

prompt: What do the students agree about the anatomy section of their presentation?

options.text: It would be better if Cath spoke about it.
It should be kept quite short.
It should be based on information from the internet.

evidence: They agree they should limit the anatomy section because they do not want to spend much time on anatomy when the main focus is treatment.
why: They explicitly agree to keep this section limited and brief, which matches option B.
trap: A: They discuss who has notes and downloaded material, but the key agreement is about length, not simply who presents it. C: Cath has lecture notes and a handout, while the other student has downloaded material; they do not agree that the section should be based on internet information.
explanation: The anatomy section should be brief so most presentation time can be spent on treatment.

prompt: What do the students agree to include in the last section?
evidence: They suggest that in the final section the two of them could show how some of the therapies actually work.
why: Showing how therapies work means demonstrating treatment, so option B is correct.
trap: A: Their final-section agreement is about showing therapies in action, not adding injury visuals. C: Patient interviews are not the agreed activity for this section.
explanation: The final section will include practical demonstrations of how treatments work.
